name: svgbob
desc: Convert your ascii diagram scribbles into happy little SVG
why: Turns ASCII diagram sketches into clean SVG, a delightful transform from text characters into geometry.

brief.what_it_is: Svgbob is a converter that turns ASCII text diagrams into SVG images. You give it a sketch drawn with keyboard characters such as dashes, pipes, plus signs, slashes and periods, and it outputs an SVG graphic. The README describes it as providing a CLI that takes text as input and creates an SVG image as output. The homepage is a browser-based editor demo of the same idea.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's framing is simple: 'Svgbob can create a nice graphical representation of your text diagrams.' The point is to keep diagrams as plain text that is easy to write and diff, while still getting clean vector graphics out of them.
brief.how_it_works: Each character is interpreted according to its neighbours, not in isolation. The specification gives examples: a period becomes a rounded corner when a line connects to it from below and from the right, a plus sign becomes a sharp corner or an intersection depending on how many perpendicular lines meet it, and a letter v becomes an arrowhead when a line comes in from above. Double quotes act as an escape so that text inside them is drawn as text rather than interpreted as drawing characters.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond brew install was described in the README. The brew formula ships two executables, svgbob and svgbob_cli. The README's crates.io and docs.rs badges suggest it is also distributed as a Rust crate, but the README gives no install or usage commands. The crates.io page returned a 404 when I checked it.
brief.standout: The context-sensitive character rules are the clever part: the same '.' or '+' changes meaning depending on which lines touch it, so ordinary ASCII sketches come out as tidy curves, arrows and intersections. It is also embedded in several documentation toolchains (asciidoctor, zola, kroki, discourse, typst's bob-draw, and mdbook-svgbob for google/comprehensive-rust), which suggests it is genuinely used rather than just a demo.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a CI test badge pointing at a GitHub Actions workflow and a screenshot dated 2024-11-20, but I did not see a release date, a last-commit date, or a changelog. The crates.io page returned a 404, so I could not check the latest version date.
brief.caveats: The README contains no command examples, so usage has to be inferred from the one-sentence description of the CLI. The homepage returned only an empty editor shell with no readable text in my fetch, so I could not read what the demo shows. The specification page was cut off at 40000 characters, so I only read the first part of the character reference. I did not see license text, though the README links a LICENSE file and the crates.io license badge.
